query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex metallic alloys with marginal glass-forming ability, a single composition-tuning intervention that increases the atomic fraction of one component chosen for (i) a strongly negative pairwise mixing enthalpy with phosphorus and (ii) an atomic radius at least ~10% different from the alloy’s average will improve both glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state by strengthening P-centered chemical short-range order, lowering the liquidus, raising reduced glass transition temperature, and slowing atomic mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal transition-metal alloy containing phosphorus (typically 5–15 at.% P) that forms an amorphous structure only under high cooling rates (thin ribbons or sub-millimeter castings) and exhibits modest thermal stability (a small supercooled liquid region).
generation.intervention: At fixed overall phosphorus content, increase (by a small increment, e.g., a few atomic percent) the concentration of a single metallic component selected by the property criteria: (1) pairwise mixing enthalpy with P is strongly negative (approximately ≤ −20 kJ/mol), and (2) its atomic radius differs by ≥10% from the alloy’s average atomic radius; decrease, by the same amount, one component with weak interaction with P to keep total P and total metal fraction constant.
generation.conditions: Induction melting under inert atmosphere, rapid quenching via copper mold casting or melt spinning; identical processing between baseline and modified compositions. The intervention is applied without changing total P content or the number of principal elements; melt temperatures and times are kept the same to isolate compositional effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and stabilization of phosphorus-centered chemical short-range order clusters and heterogeneous atomic packing that increase topological and chemical frustration against crystallization.
generation.mechanism: More negative P–metal bonding enthalpy and larger local size mismatch increase melt viscosity and reduce atomic diffusivity near the liquidus; they also deepen the eutectic and lower the liquidus temperature, thereby increasing reduced glass transition temperature (Trg = Tg/Tl). These effects raise the nucleation barrier and slow crystal growth, expanding the supercooled liquid region (ΔTx) and permitting thicker amorphous sections under the same cooling rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an otherwise comparable baseline alloy (same total P and principal element count), the modified alloy will show directionally improved glass-forming ability (larger critical casting thickness at fixed cooling conditions) and improved thermal stability of the amorphous state (higher ΔTx and/or higher crystallization onset temperature). The magnitude of improvement is expected to be nontrivial but is uncertain without system-specific data.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar P-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy in which the targeted component either has weaker interaction with P (less negative mixing enthalpy) or smaller size mismatch, and which exhibits marginal GFA and modest supercooled liquid region under the same processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is unlikely to work if the selected component promotes the formation of stable crystalline phosphides near Tg (e.g., strong tendency for intermetallic phosphide precipitation), if the substitution reduces configurational complexity enough to favor ordering, if processing enables excessive segregation, or if the element is highly volatile/oxidation-prone under melting. Extremely low P content (insufficient P-centered CSRO) or excessively high P content (embrittlement, phase separation) may also negate the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: No eligible prior evidence is provided here; thus, the expected direction of improvement is stated qualitatively and the effect size cannot be specified. Outcomes will depend on the specific element set and interactions in the chosen alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy series that differ only in the targeted component: Series A incrementally increases the fraction of a component meeting the property criteria (strongly negative P mixing enthalpy and ≥10% size mismatch) while decreasing a weakly P-interacting component by the same amount; Series B performs the opposite change. Keep total P constant and processing identical. Cast rods at fixed diameters and produce melt-spun ribbons to assess GFA and thermal stability.
measurements: Critical casting thickness (max amorphous diameter at fixed cooling protocol)
DSC-derived Tg, Tx, and Tl to compute ΔTx and Trg
High-energy XRD or synchrotron PDF to quantify changes in P-centered short-range order (peak positions/intensities consistent with CSRO)
High-temperature viscosity near Tl (e.g., oscillating cup or beam-bending methods)
Isothermal crystallization kinetics (TTT curves) to extract nucleation and growth rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across at least three independent melts per composition, the intervention fails to produce statistically significant (p < 0.05) improvements in either critical casting thickness or ΔTx (and does not lower Tl or increase Trg) relative to the baseline, or if structural measurements show no increase in P-centered short-range order, the hypothesis is falsified.
